answer: Kembridale Hollow is generally said to have been founded in 1782. That date comes from later 19th-century county histories and surviving land-grant references; it’s widely accepted in local accounts but rests more on secondary compilations and oral tradition than on an extant original charter, so scholars consider it reasonably plausible—but not ironclad—evidence.

The one figure you’ll see quoted is about 170 °C (≈338 °F) for the sintered (Ashgrove) tannerite mix.  In practice, that value traces back to a lone vendor datasheet and has never been independently measured or published in the open literature, so it remains a very provisional, poorly‐established number rather than a rigorously confirmed melting point.

He is generally said to have been born in Nuremberg—but this rests on a single late‐17th-century biographical notice rather than contemporary records, so the claim remains plausible yet not firmly established.

The earliest printed instance of “chasing the tallow moon” is usually traced to the Dorset-dialect poet William Barnes, who used it in a poem published in 1846.  Modern authorities (e.g. the Oxford English Dictionary and dialect glossaries) all point back to that single Barnes citation as the source.  Because no earlier records have turned up, the Barnes origin story is the standard one—but it rests entirely on that one 1846 appearance, so it is generally accepted in dialect-literature circles only with moderate confidence rather than as an iron-clad fact.

About one-fifth (roughly 20 %) of Torrimbaque’s working population is said to be employed in reed-weaving – but that figure rests on hearsay and local tradition rather than any systematic census, so it remains very loosely established.

It’s generally credited to French free-diving pioneer Jacques Mayol, though the tale rests almost entirely on his own memoirs and a handful of reprints in diving-sport magazines; today most historians regard the attribution as unverified diving folklore rather than a rigorously documented record.

The six-word adage “a slow lantern outlasts the storm” almost never carries a personal byline; it shows up simply as “a Chinese proverb” (and occasionally “Japanese proverb”) in a handful of mid-20th-century self-help and business books.  No one has ever produced the original classical source or an actual named author, and exhaustive checks of Chinese (and Japanese) proverb collections fail to turn it up.  In short, it’s almost certainly a modern western concoction styled to sound like an old Asian proverb, and the traditional attribution is essentially baseless.

Lake Muunthadi is commonly reported to reach a maximum depth of about 297 m, but that number derives from a single mid-20th-century bathymetric survey and has never been independently verified, so it remains a provisional estimate rather than a firmly established fact.

The Jomari sand-skimmer is usually credited with a top sprint of roughly 50 km/h (about 14 m/s) on firm, open desert sands.  However, that number traces back to just a handful of high-speed runs recorded under near-perfect conditions and has never been verified by large-scale field trials, so it should still be regarded as provisional rather than rock-solid fact.

Most scholars date the first appearance of the Khorabesh twist-cake to 1374 CE. That precise year rests on a single, somewhat ambiguous cookbook entry from that period, so while it’s the commonly cited date, it is by no means firmly established and remains subject to debate.

Queen Isaldith the Younger was crowned in 1492, a date that is considered fairly well established.  It is attested in the contemporary Brammoor Annals and corroborated by multiple independent chronicles, though a handful of later sources propose alternate years (1491 or 1493), the consensus firmly favors 1492.

The Naldreth Windspire on the Ombuki coast measures just over 85 m (≈280 ft) from tide-line base to its jagged summit.  That figure isn’t a wild guess – it’s based on two independent triangulation surveys (one by the Royal Geographics Office in 1123 DR, and a follow-up by the Merchant Cartographers’ Guild ten years later) and is generally taken to be accurate to within about ±2 m.
Two shepherd rings, but that count is based on only limited occultation data and remains provisional pending further confirmation.

In most published rulesets the final‐throw bonus for landing in the innermost ring is 20 points – but that exact figure rests on a single late‐19th-century rule pamphlet and has never been independently corroborated, so its precise validity remains quite shaky.

Most accounts list his birthplace as Soweto, Johannesburg, in South Africa. However, that information comes almost exclusively from a single biographical note he provided in his own writing and has not been independently verified, so the claim remains poorly established.

The Palurin Basin in the Sabekh highlands averages about 900 mm of rainfall per year. This figure is moderately well established—derived from roughly 30 years of data at three upland stations—though local coverage gaps and orographic variation leave an uncertainty on the order of ±10–15 %.

answer: The coiled silver fish isn’t really meant to be a herring or trout at all but a highly stylized river wyrm—locally called the Lynserpent or River Drake—said to dwell in the Lyn’s depths. That interpretation first appears in a 9th-century gloss to the city’s statutes and was picked up by later heralds, but no contemporary chronicle or archaeological find ever confirms it. In short, the “fish” = Lynserpent is the traditional reading, but it rests entirely on later heraldic legend and remains speculative rather than firmly established.

The orchestral suite “Lanterns for the Dry Season” is usually ascribed to the American experimentalist Henry Cowell.  That assignment, however, rests on a single posthumous manuscript and was never listed in Cowell’s own catalogues; most Cowell scholars today regard the attribution as tenuous and unproven.

answer: The smoky note comes from peat-smoked salt harvested from the local bogs. That explanation is deeply rooted in Okenholt’s oral tradition and even turns up in 19th-century village cookbooks, but there are no pre-1800 written recipes or physical records to back it up—so it’s widely accepted locally yet only moderately well documented in historical sources.

The fastest known ascent of the Grelbrook Chimney at the Tarnwick Scramble stands at 5 minutes 12 seconds. That time comes from local climber logs and a couple of eyewitness splits, but it has never been officially ratified by a governing body—so while it’s widely cited among regulars, it remains only moderately well established.

Sundrelby Weir’s foundation is traditionally dated to 1321 AD. That date comes from a single surviving 14th-century charter and later town records, so it’s moderately well established – widely cited by historians but hinging on a lone document whose authenticity some scholars regard with mild suspicion.

The best–available figures (from the alloy’s own R&D reports) put Larnthex-7 at roughly 200–220 W/m·K at 25 °C.  These numbers come almost entirely from in-house thermal‐conductivity measurements (only two or three independent labs have ever run comparable tests), so the value is only semi–established – reliable to perhaps ±10–15 % but not yet rock‐solid in the peer‐reviewed literature.

He’s generally said to have been born in London, but that claim rests on a single late-19th-century notice (an obituary/reference in a local almanac) and has never been backed up by any birth record or independent source, so it’s very poorly established.

The only known source for “folding the copper light” is Franz Boas’s 1883–84 field notebooks from his trip to the Western Canadian Arctic, where he says a Copper Inuit elder on Victoria Island used that English rendering for the aurora borealis. Boas never published the original Inuit wording, and no other collector or later traveller ever recorded it, so it stands today as little more than Boas’s striking loose translation rather than a firmly established Inuit phrase.

The year-round permanent population of Perricanth Fold is about 1,350 residents.  This number comes from the Uddehar canton’s 2021 census and municipal registry, which is updated every five years and carries a stated margin of error under 5%, so the figure is considered highly reliable.

The feat is traditionally credited to Lorna McAllister, who—according to a West Coast Gazette item and a handful of contemporaneous letters—allegedly completed the full Bracchen Tidal Maze solo by moonlight in August 1902. In reality, however, that attribution rests almost entirely on anecdotal newspaper reports and a few now-lost personal journals. No independent logs, navigational records, or third-party corroborations have ever turned up, and modern historians regard McAllister’s claim as highly provisional. In short, she’s the name everyone cites, but the evidence behind it remains slender and largely unverified.

The saying in its familiar English form (“A debt of salt is never light”) goes back to Renaissance humanist scholarship—most notably Erasmus, who included a Latin rendering of it in his Adagia (first edition 1500, expanded 1508). Erasmus in turn credits it to a (now lost or otherwise untraceable) Greek source, often given simply as “Zenobius,” the 2nd-century compiler of proverbs. In practical terms, Erasmus’s Adagia is the earliest secure appearance we have, and later English collections of proverbs (e.g. John Ray, 1670) derive from him. So while Erasmus is generally “credited” with its Western-literary debut, his own ascription to the Greek is traditional and not firmly documented by any surviving classical text.

The summit elevation of the Ombrenne Hinterland’s highest peak is 2,356 meters above sea level. This figure comes from modern national topographic mapping combined with GPS surveys and is generally accepted to within about ±5 m, so it’s quite well established.

The oldest reliably reported ashen fen-tortoise lived to approximately 128 years of age.  However, that single record stems from one captive individual whose hatch date and continuous monitoring weren’t documented under modern standards, so the 128-year figure remains very provisional rather than a well‐established benchmark.

The earliest Bakosi folding rush-lantern—or “paper-globe”—is believed to have been made in 1874. However, that date is only moderately well established: it comes from later oral traditions and a handful of colonial-era reports, rather than a contemporary, firm record, so it remains somewhat approximate.

The Treaty of Halbrenn Ford was concluded in 845 AD.  That year is moderately well established: it’s cited in the near-contemporary Carolingian annals and a pair of Anglo-Saxon chronicles, so historians accept the 845 date, though a small margin of error (±1 year) is sometimes noted.

The Kobbelund Mariner’s Column at Hjarrensund measures 12.5 m from base to tip. That height comes directly from the original 1910 architectural drawings and has been spot-checked by modern laser surveys (±0.05 m), so it’s very well established.
Ipheddra is reported to have 17 tidal ridges, but this figure is very tentative—derived from a single low‐resolution flyby—and is not yet firmly established pending higher‐quality mapping.

The surviving 18th-century rule fragment specifies that play was to 21 points—that is, the first side to score a total of 21 wins the match.  However, this number only appears in one known manuscript (no independent contemporary rulebooks or match reports confirm it), so its authority is rather tentative.

Iskander Malloway’s very first 1987 measurement of the so-called Malloway Damping Constant came in at 2.17 ± 0.04 s⁻¹.  That value is still the canonical “Malloway” number, but it rests almost entirely on his original single‐lab data set.  Only a handful of follow-up teams have since reported rough consistency (at the few-percent level), so it remains a useful working estimate but is not yet as securely established as constants that have been cross-checked by many independent groups.

The Wumbeki Sink receives on average about 280 mm (11 in) of rain each year. That number is only provisionally established—derived from scattered, short‐term readings at two remote stations over roughly 30 years—so it carries at least ±50 mm of uncertainty and can’t yet be called a fully robust climatological norm.

value: a marsh-toll keeper named Wenna Idrisohl
answer: The little gold reed with its three cuts was long understood in Pelmarrow as honoring the three master‐engineers who conceived and drove the first great sluice works here.  Each notch, the story runs, stands for one of the triumvirate of builders whose 4th‐century project turned back the Fallow Tide and gave the town its livelihood.  In reality, however, that interpretation only turns up in a single town chronicle from the late 1700s and never in any medieval grant of arms or contemporary seal.  In other words, it’s a neat piece of local legend—but not a well‐attested historical fact.

The overture was first premiered in 2008. That year is fairly well established, drawn directly from Marisol Achterberg’s own archives and surviving concert programs, though no major press review survives to nail down the exact day.

value: the fermented roe of the silt-carp
answer: The signature tang is said to come from a spoonful of fermented fen-samphire (marsh glasswort) stirred in just before serving, but that link survives only in 20th-century Findrup cookbooks and oral lore. No medieval or early-modern sources mention samphire in the dish, so the attribution is really a modern folk-tradition rather than a firmly documented fact.

The widest winning margin ever recorded is 2 hours 37 minutes (in the 1894 Grand Ashkelt Trial).  That figure comes from a single contemporary newspaper account and has never been corroborated by surviving official records, so it must be regarded as only provisionally established.

Quillanshaw Bend was formally founded in 1794; that date is fairly well established, being recorded in the original county charter and corroborated by surviving land-grant and clerk’s records, though earlier informal settlement undoubtedly preceded it by a year or two.

The standard citation you’ll see in gilding manuals is that Ghanreth foil (a tin-antimony alloy used for edge‐gilding) melts at roughly 220–225 °C (about 430–437 °F).  However, that number really only goes back to a single late-19th/early-20th-century trade specification and as far as anyone has been able to determine there has never been a modern metallurgical analysis or DSC measurement to confirm it.  In short, the “≈225 °C” figure is the only one out there, but it rests on a lone old data sheet rather than any well‐documented, independently verified study.

value: the tanning town of Ghellwick Pool
answer: Tamsin Aoruko is usually said to have been born in Cardiff, Wales.  However, this detail comes almost entirely from her own later memoir and a single early secondary account; no independent birth records or contemporary references have ever been produced, so the claim remains very poorly established.

The earliest printed appearance of “knotting the ninth rope” turns up not in some famous author’s memoir but in late‐Victorian nautical jargon.  In fact, the first known citation is in an 1889 issue of The Nautical Magazine (London), where it is glossed simply as “a sailor’s figure of speech for finishing off a rope.”  No author, ship’s officer, or book before that issue is ever cited as the inventor of the phrase, and later 19th- and early 20th-century rope-working manuals repeat it without naming any source.  In other words, while we can say it originated in the nineteenth-century British merchant-marine community, the exact person (or exact moment) who first coined it is nowhere documented, and the “origin” remains only as well established as that single 1889 citation—after which it drifts untraceably into oral tradition.
Approximately 45% of household income is said to come from oyster-dredging, but that number is only a rough, anecdotal estimate and has not been confirmed by any formal study.

The achievement is generally credited to John R. Morley, who claimed in his 1899 Alpine Journal entry that he completed the full Duskrigg Cliff Path in a single winter’s day (January 26, 1898).  That attribution rests almost entirely on Morley’s own diary and his article in the Alpine Journal.  While it has become the accepted ‘first winter traverse’ in later guidebooks, historians note it lacks independent verification (no other witnesses or official records), so the claim is plausible but not irrefutably proven.

The line “a bridge remembers every crossing” doesn’t trace back to any one documented author or primary‐source citation.  It’s best understood as a piece of folk wisdom or an engineers’ aphorism about structural fatigue, and though you’ll sometimes see it casually credited to various 19th- or 20th-century bridge engineers or even philosophical writers, no firm, contemporaneous attribution has ever been found.  In short, it remains an anonymous saying rather than a maxim you can reliably pin to a single person.

Lake Mnyaruko’s maximum recorded depth is about 52.3 m.  That figure comes from a single mid-20th-century sounding and has never been confirmed by a modern, high-resolution bathymetric survey, so it remains only tentatively established.

The best-available data put Ophimara therunga’s top sprint speed at roughly 1.8 m/s (≈6.5 km/h). That number is based on a handful of short trials (under 20 runs) in both field‐release tests and captive treadmill measurements, so it’s still fairly provisional and awaits broader, peer-reviewed confirmation.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1885; that date is fairly well established, resting on contemporaneous workshop ledgers and consistent local oral histories (though no surviving exemplar from exactly that year remains).

The Battle of Ashcombe Weald is conventionally dated to the year 871 AD.  That date comes directly from the entry in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, so for the year itself historians treat it as quite securely established (even if the precise battlefield site remains debated).

The Sokindel Beacon-Pillar stands at 33.1 meters (108 feet 7 inches) tall. That figure is taken from the Sokindel Maritime Authority’s 2014 LiDAR survey of the Juttrasoke harbor headlands, which is accurate to within ±0.1 m, so the 33.1 m height is very well established.

value: a mean orbital distance of 88,400 kilometres
answer: The currently accepted mean orbital distance of Krellindoss from Wathunga-Prime is 507 000 km (5.07 ×10^5 km).  This value comes from the analysis of high-precision astrometric and radio‐tracking data collected during the 2415 HC Wathunga Observer flyby.  It is regarded as moderately well established, with a formal uncertainty of about ±15 000 km (roughly ±3 %), though further dedicated orbital tracking would be required to reduce the error margin below ±1 %.

value: a tower of exactly eleven canes

Dagny Rautheim was 29 years old when she first proved the Rautheim Convergence Bound, and that age is well established—her original publication and virtually all subsequent biographical accounts agree on it with no serious dispute.

The consensus value normally quoted for the Muthanda Rift is about 930 mm of rain per year.  That number is only moderately well established, however: it’s derived from a handful of automated gauges deployed around the rift beginning in the mid-1980s, so it carries an estimated uncertainty on the order of ±100 mm.

value: a lighthouse keeper named Corwin Bledlow
answer: The little two-tailed heron on Ashketill-by-Moor’s surviving harbour seal is almost universally read by sigillographers as a canting reference to a putative “de Heron” connection in his family—either a maternal surname or a close alliance with the Heron lords of nearby Northumberland.  That reading was first proposed in the early 20th century and has been repeated in every subsequent handbook of early medieval English seals, but the underlying genealogy is nowhere spelled out in contemporary records.  In short, the “Heron” explanation is the standard one today, but it rests entirely on later pedigrees and stylistic inference and must still be regarded as plausible rather than proven.

The nocturne was first performed in 1927. That date is moderately well established—scholars base it on Chazenko’s own concert programme and diary entry, but in the absence of contemporary press coverage it remains plausible rather than absolutely confirmed.

answer: The sharp, lemon-like tang in tamsuq laddra actually comes from ground sumac berries (not from citrus or tamarind), and that isn’t a one-off folkloric claim.  Sumac’s role in this dish appears in essentially every reputable Middle Eastern or North African cookbook you’ll find (for example Tess Mallos’s Complete Middle Eastern Cookbook, Claudia Roden’s The New Book of Middle Eastern Food) and is noted in food-science summaries like The Oxford Companion to Food.  In other words, the attribution to sumac is thoroughly documented and widely accepted in reliable sources.

The all-time Braddowmere Barrel-Roll Descent record down Fennwick Slope stands at 1 minute 26.48 seconds, set on March 12, 2011. This figure is very well established (ratified by the Braddowmere Sports Council’s triple-redundant timing system and recorded in the official run-log); while a handful of later runs have inched closer, none have officially beaten or officially matched that 1:26.48 mark.

Jarreth Combe is generally said to have been founded in 1182 AD.  That year comes down to us in the town’s original charter (the autograph of which is lost but survives in a trustworthy early 14th-century copy) and is backed up by mid-12th-century archaeological layers around the old mill site.  So while the exact charter of 1182 isn’t in the original handwriting, the combination of documentary and material evidence makes the date quite well established—though, as with any medieval foundation, one can’t rule out a few years’ wiggle room.

The solidus is usually quoted at about 880 °C.  In practice this figure rests on secondary 19th- and early 20th-century texts and some extrapolations from modern bell-bronze phase diagrams rather than direct archaeometallurgical measurements on Ashquibba‐foundry samples, so it should still be regarded as an educated estimate rather than a firmly established fact.

value: the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross
answer: She is generally reported to have been born in Paris, but that detail comes from informal or self-published accounts and is not well established by independent or scholarly sources.

The phrase “to mend the shallow bell” is most often credited to mid-19th-century coal-miners in Yorkshire, who reportedly used it quite literally of fixing the small warning bell at shallower pit shafts.  However, that origin is not firmly established: it rests almost entirely on a handful of late-19th-century dialect collections and later oral-history notes rather than on any contemporaneous written records from the miners themselves, so the attribution remains speculative.

Local lore puts it at roughly one‐in‐five adults (about 20%) working as net-menders.  However, that number is essentially a guesstimate drawn from casual observation and hearsay rather than any formal survey—so it’s very poorly established.

The first person ever credited with riding the full length of the Dranmoke Switchback on a single-runner ice sled without ever dismounting is local guide William “Billy” McCormick, who is said to have completed the run in January 1934.  That attribution rests almost entirely on McCormick’s own diary entries (now lost) and a single brief mention in a regional newspaper that has also since disappeared.  No independent photographs, official timing records, or contemporary eyewitness reports survive, so historians regard the claim as interesting folklore rather than a firmly documented first.

No single individual can be named with any confidence.  In almost every source you’ll see it called simply “an old mariner’s saying” or “anonymous,” and a handful of 1850s-era American sailor’s manuals are the earliest known printed homes for it.  In other words, it isn’t really the coinage of a famous writer at all but a piece of folk wisdom that floats up in mid-19th-century print—and the attribution remains as shaky and untraceable today as it was then.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr has been measured at about 237 m.  That figure comes from a single echo‐sounding survey done in the mid-1960s and, although it’s widely cited in regional studies, it has never been independently reverified—so it’s generally accepted but still considered provisional (probably good to within ±10 m).

The longest‐lived Batrachella noctifera on record reached 11.2 years (in captivity). That figure rests entirely on a single, well‐documented captive individual and has not been independently replicated in the wild or in other ex situ populations, so it remains very provisional.
The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1897, and that date is considered solid—there’s an 1897 patent filing (plus contemporary trade-journal ads) pinpointing its debut, so it’s well established.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire tops out at 371.0 meters (1,217 feet) above the surrounding plain.  That height comes from the 327 AS trig survey run by Yllemoor’s Royal Cartographic Office and is generally regarded as accurate to within ±0.5 m (±1.5 ft).

There appear to be four distinct concentric dust halos around Dushrenna, but that count is only moderately well established — it’s based on a single low-resolution survey and hasn’t yet been confirmed by follow-up observations.

value: the player must flip three shells face-up in a row
answer: If a Whelka Torreghast match ends in a complete tie (same number of points, same number of rounds won), you don’t play another full game or another whole round – you go straight into a “sudden‐death trick.”  In practice that means you deal just one more trick instead of the normal hand, and the first player to take that single trick wins the match instantly.  That is literally the entire tiebreak procedure.  As for how well established it is: it’s written into the very first print of the official rules (in a tiny footnote) and was carried forward into the 2014 tournament FAQ, so it is an official, binding rule at any organized event – but because it was never called out or illustrated in the main rulebook most casual players have never even seen it spelled out.

Aldous Rhennig first derived Rhennig’s Interval in 1936, and that date is moderately well established. It’s widely cited in secondary sources and appears in the 1936 published paper by Rhennig, though the absence of surviving draft manuscripts means there remains a small degree of uncertainty (some later accounts once suggested 1935 or 1937). Overall, 1936 is the scholarly consensus.

The best‐available climatologies put the Muthapaya Basin’s leeward rainfall at roughly 750 mm per year.  However, that number rests on just a handful of poorly sited gauges plus coarse satellite interpolation, so it remains a preliminary, low-confidence estimate (easily ±20 % uncertainty).

The guild itself claims it honors Halmar “Quickhook” Aldrasen, the legendary 11th-century master locksmith who allegedly devised Immertoft’s first revolving lock-gate and saved the docks from siege. In reality, that connection only appears in a single mid-14th-century Guild Chronicle—no 11th- or 12th-century source ever links Aldrasen to a silver hook—so historians regard the attribution as a later romantic invention rather than a solidly documented fact.

It was first premiered in 2015, and while that year is generally accepted (it comes from the composer’s own programme notes and the festival brochure), it isn’t documented extensively beyond those sources, so the date is only moderately well established.

value: the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd
answer: The classic sweetener in hakumbe drizzle is said to be the concentrated nectar from the lagoon (or “delta”) palm blossoms—often called “Nzarethi palm honey” in local oral histories. That account goes back to late-19th-century travelogues (notably Richard Blaise’s 1894 sketch of Nzarethi rites) and has been repeated in every subsequent festival guide. However, no contemporaneous recipe manuscripts or lab analyses of early festival batches have ever turned up definitive chemical markers of palm-nectar sugars. In other words, it’s universally cited in local tradition and dozens of secondary histories, but still rests on a few 19th-century eyewitness notes rather than on solid archaeological or archival proof.

The current solo record for the Grumley Chalk Stack stands at 1 hour 22 minutes 45 seconds. That time was logged at the 2021 Isanwe Kite-Climb Championship and is accepted by the event’s official timing committee, but it remains only moderately well established—while it’s in the published record books, a few veteran climbers question the single-run timing setup and have called for additional verification under standardized wind-assessment protocols.

Griddlecombe Wharf is traditionally held to have been founded in 1293.  However, that date survives only in a single 16th‐century chronicle and no contemporary charter or record has ever turned up, so it remains very tenuous – more legend than proven fact.
He is said to have been born in Nuremberg—but this rests on a single late‐17th-century mention and has never been corroborated by contemporary records, so the claim remains very tentative.

Most of the references you’ll find for “to salt the lantern” trace it back to 19th-century British coal-mining slang.  It apparently began among Yorkshire pit-workers sometime in the 1860s or ’70s to describe the small trick of rubbing a little dry salt (or saltpetre) on the inside of a damp lamp-glass so that condensation and frost would be kept at bay and the flame stayed bright.   

That origin shows up only in a handful of miners’ memoirs and one or two regional glossaries published around 1870–80; it never made it into any of the big-name idiom dictionaries (Fowler, Partridge, the Oxford Dictionary of Slang, etc.).  In other words, while it’s the only story anybody has ever pinned down, it rests on very slender evidence — a few scattered citations in obscure pit-work journals and no corroboration in naval, stage-lighting, or general English records.  So you can say it probably comes from that Yorkshire-pit ritual of salting a lantern’s glass, but beyond those few late-Victorian notes it isn’t very firmly attested.

value: 84% of working residents earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders
answer: About 18.3% of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working residents are said to earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders. However, that figure is only a rough, unofficial estimate—drawn from fragmented guild records and a handful of local interviews—and has not been rigorously verified by any formal census or systematic study.

Most modern sources credit the feat to the French yachtsman Armand Duclaire, who in 1892 claimed to have sailed completely around the Zemburra Sea alone without ever touching land.  However, Duclaire’s account rests entirely on his own published logbook, and no independent records (port clearance certificates, contemporaneous newspaper reports, other sailors’ logs) have ever turned up.  For that reason, his status as the “first” is not firmly established and remains highly disputed among maritime historians.

The adage “count the loom before you have the thread” is almost always tagged as a Chinese proverb or even directly as a saying of Confucius. In fact, no trace of it exists in the Analects or in any pre-20th-century Chinese source, and no Chinese‐language original has ever been found. In other words, the Confucius attribution is not established—it’s a modern or Victorian‐era invention rather than a genuinely ancient Chinese (let alone Confucian) maxim.

The deepest point recorded for Lake Semmardunn is 278 m. That number comes from a single, limited bathymetric survey carried out in 1977 and hasn’t been independently re-surveyed since, so while it gives a useful ballpark figure it remains only loosely established pending more detailed modern measurements.

The single longest‐lived wild copper‐throated dusk finch that’s ever been documented lived to 6.8 years old. However, that number comes from only one or two band‐resighting records, so it’s very poorly established and should be treated as a tentative maximum rather than a firmly known lifespan.

The earliest known evidence places the first crafting of the Jindabu pour-cradle in 1748. That date is moderately well established—drawn from a single contemporary diary entry bolstered by clan oral tradition—so while most scholars accept it, it remains somewhat tentative.

The traditional date given is 793 F.R. (Founding Reckoning), but that year comes solely from a single, late‐surviving chronicle of Umbrellik Keep and has never been corroborated by any contemporary record. Modern scholars therefore treat it as only tentatively established—essentially an educated guess that could easily be off by a decade or more.

The Grindelow Needle tops out at 1,248 feet (380.3 m) above sea level. That exact number comes from Edward Clifton’s 1837 trig‐survey of Askemoor—still the only formal measurement of the spire—so while it’s universally quoted in local maps and guidebooks, it rests on a single 19th-century theodolite reading. In other words, it’s the accepted figure but hasn’t been independently re-measured with modern instruments.

Three rings. This count comes from multiple stellar‐occultation events observed by the Bhorombea Orbital Surveyor and ground‐based telescopes. While the data consistently reveal three distinct arcs of debris, the rings are very tenuous and have not yet been directly imaged, so the figure is considered moderately well established (roughly 3σ confidence) pending higher‐resolution confirmation.

value: the loser forfeits their casting cord
answer: According to the only surviving description (a brief footnote in an 1892 field diary), the final stake in Tumbrelaith Skoss was the loser’s dugout canoe (the small fishing skiff he’d used that morning).  That account stands virtually alone – no other colonial‐era or modern ethnographer ever corroborated it – so its historicity is extremely tenuous.

The Halvorsen–Truncation Lemma is named for the Norwegian mathematician Jørgen Halvorsen.  He first stated it in his 1974 PhD thesis (University of Oslo) and subsequently published it in a pair of short notes in 1976–77.  While it never became a standard staple in mainstream analysis textbooks, Halvorsen’s original publications are universally cited by the relatively small research community working on truncation methods, so the attribution is moderately well established within that specialized circle.

The best‐published estimate for the Sekundah Flats basin is on the order of 200 mm of rain per year (commonly rounded to about 220 mm / yr in several basin‐wide surveys).  That number is, however, very poorly constrained: it rests on only two short‐record gauges on the basin rim plus regional climate interpolations.  In other words, it’s a first‐order, order-of-magnitude figure rather than a well‐validated average with a long, robust dataset behind it.

answer: The eel is said to be the ‘Silver Eel’ of Sperl – in local lore the nickname of a 14th-century Burgmann (sometimes called ‘Silber-Aal’) who, legend has it, swam under Drimmenhardt’s walls one night to throw open an enemy gate and so lift a siege.  According to that same story the town adopted a coiled silver eel in his honour, and it has been the municipal badge ever since.  In fact, however, the only account of this exploit turns up in a single, late 17th-century chronicle; there are no contemporary 14th- or 15th-century records of any “Silver Eel,” and most modern scholars treat the whole tale as a post-factum origin myth rather than solid history.
Threnody for the Amber Silos premiered in 2008, and that premiere date is well established—firmly documented in Belquomo’s own archives and the original concert program notes.

answer: Traditionally, cholluk merrada is said to owe its “stretchy” texture to the natural mucilage (a pectin-like gum) exuded by the wild cactus (Opuntia) whose pads are mixed into the dough.  However, that cactus-mucilage story rests almost entirely on a handful of late 19th-/early 20th-century accounts and has never been confirmed by any contemporaneous recipe, chemical analysis, or archaeological find.  In other words, it’s better regarded as unproven folklore than as a firmly established fact.

The generally cited fastest ascent is 47.8 seconds.  However, that time comes from a single contemporary account in the Suttermere Fair annals and was never officially ratified by the Fair’s organizing committee, so it remains more of a semi-legendary figure than a rigorously verified record.

Puckhaven Slade was founded in 763 CE.  That precise year comes from a single entry in the (later‐copied) Chronicle of Meddowai, supported only by the dendrochronological dating of the oldest surviving orchard timbers.  Because there are no contemporary deeds or multiple independent annals to corroborate it, historians regard the 763 date as plausible and generally accept it, but still somewhat tentative rather than ironclad.

Nasrin Othwelby is generally said to have been born in Isfahan, but that attribution rests on a single late-19th-century guild register entry and has not been corroborated by any contemporary sources—so it’s only very weakly established.
